gloss: fine flour, the choice part of wheat meal
summary: סֹלֶת is fine flour: the choice part of wheat meal (סֹלֶת חִטִּים, Exo 29:2), set apart from ordinary meal, קֶמַח, at Solomon's table and worth twice its measure of barley in Samaria's market (1Ki 5:2; 2Ki 7:1). It is food for an honoured guest and a king, and the food Yahweh gave Jerusalem with oil and honey (Gen 18:6; Ezk 16:13, 19). Almost all its uses are the grain offering, the shewbread and the measured flour that goes with each sacrifice, mixed with oil, as on the day of the עֹמֶר and in the two loaves of the firstfruits (Lev 2:1; 23:13, 17; 24:5; Num 28–29). Aramaic סֻלְתָּא, Akkadian siltu, groats, and Arabic sult, a husk-less grain, share the word.

words.summary: The one word of the root in scripture. The database files it under סלק by BDB's page order; its own consonants are סלת, and no verb of the root occurs in scripture.

senses.gloss: fine flour, choice wheat meal (as food)
senses.definition: Flour of wheat, the finer part of the meal: distinguished from common meal (קֶמַח) and from barley, and so the food of a feast, a king's table and a favoured bride.

evidence.note: “סֹלֶת חִטִּים you shall make them”: fine flour of wheat.
“Three seahs of קֶמַח סֹלֶת”: meal that is fine flour, kneaded into cakes for the three visitors.
Solomon's bread for one day: “thirty kors of סֹלֶת and sixty kors of קֶמַח”, the fine flour counted apart from the common meal.
“A seah of סֹלֶת for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel”: fine flour worth twice its measure of barley.
Fulfilled when the camp of Aram was plundered.
Jerusalem adorned with gold and silver and fine linen: “סֹלֶת and honey and oil you ate”, food of royalty (“you prospered to a kingdom”).
“My bread which I gave you, סֹלֶת and oil and honey I fed you”, set before idols for a pleasing smell.
Leaven hidden in “three σάτα of meal”, the measure Sarah kneaded (Gen 18:6).

senses.gloss: fine flour of the grain offering
senses.definition: The fine flour brought to Yahweh: the stuff of the מִנְחָה, the shewbread and the firstfruit loaves, measured in tenths of an ephah to each sacrifice and mostly mixed or anointed with oil, of which a handful is burnt on the altar as its memorial and the rest is the priests'.

evidence.note: “When a soul brings an offering, a מִנְחָה to Yahweh, סֹלֶת shall be his offering; he shall pour oil on it and put frankincense on it.”
The priest takes a handful “of its fine flour and of its oil” with all its frankincense and burns its memorial on the altar.
Baked in an oven: cakes of סֹלֶת, unleavened, mixed with oil, or wafers anointed with oil.
On the griddle: סֹלֶת mixed with oil, unleavened.
The poorest man's sin offering, a tenth of an ephah of סֹלֶת, with no oil and no frankincense, “for it is a sin offering”.
The anointed priest's offering, a tenth of an ephah of סֹלֶת continually, half in the morning and half in the evening.
With the thanksgiving sacrifice, cakes and wafers and סֹלֶת soaked (מֻרְבֶּכֶת).
With each lamb of the continual burnt offering, a tenth of סֹלֶת mixed with a fourth of a hin of beaten oil.
The cleansing of the leper: three tenths of סֹלֶת; one tenth for the poor man (Lev 14:21).
On the day of the waving of the עֹמֶר, the grain offering with the lamb: “two tenths of סֹלֶת mixed with oil, a fire offering to Yahweh”.
At the feast of weeks, “two loaves of waving, of two tenths; סֹלֶת they shall be, baked with leaven, firstfruits to Yahweh”.
The bread of the arrangement: “take סֹלֶת and bake it, twelve cakes”, two tenths in each.
The Nazirite's basket of unleavened cakes of סֹלֶת.
Each leader's silver dish and basin “full of סֹלֶת mixed with oil for a grain offering”; repeated for all twelve (Num 7:19–79).
With the bull at the cleansing of the Levites.
The scale for every sacrifice: a tenth of סֹלֶת for a lamb, two tenths for a ram, three tenths for a bull (Num 15:4–9).
The continual offering, a tenth of an ephah of סֹלֶת mixed with beaten oil.
In Ezekiel's house, a sixth of an ephah with a third of a hin of oil “to moisten the סֹלֶת”: dry flour to be wetted.
Levites appointed over the vessels and over the סֹלֶת, the wine, the oil, the frankincense and the spices.
The Levites' charge: the bread of the arrangement, the סֹלֶת for the grain offering, the wafers, the griddle and every measure.

evidence.locator: Gen.18.6, Lev.2.1, Lev.23.13, Lev.23.17, 1Ki.5.2: סֹלֶת → σεμίδαλις; σεμίδαλις renders סֹלֶת ×44 in the alignment

evidence.note: Among the merchandise of Babylon no one buys any more: “oil and σεμίδαλιν and wheat”, fine flour beside the grain it is made from.

parallels.note: Oil, mixed with it (בְּלוּלָה בַשֶּׁמֶן), poured on it, or eaten with it.
Honey, with fine flour and oil the rich food Yahweh gave Jerusalem.

opposites.note: Common meal, counted apart from fine flour at Solomon's table; barley meal (קֶמַח שְׂעֹרִים), not סֹלֶת, is the jealousy offering, with no oil or frankincense.
Barley, sold at half the price of fine flour.

cognates.gloss: a husk-less barley (or grain between wheat and barley), smooth like wheat
cognates.note: A grain named for having no husk; the same consonants applied to cleaned grain.

cognates.gloss: wipe off, scrape off, strip away; cut off
cognates.note: If sult is grain with its husk stripped off, this verb is the root's older sense, and סֹלֶת would be meal cleared of bran; nothing in scripture shows how the flour was made, so this stays possible.

doctrine.statement: A man too poor for two turtledoves or two young pigeons may bring a tenth of an ephah of סֹלֶת as his sin offering, with no oil and no frankincense; the priest burns a handful of it on the altar “on Yahweh's fire offerings”, makes a covering for him, and “it shall be forgiven him” (Lev 5:11–13). So the law itself left a way back for the poorest, and is why the letter to the Hebrews says “almost all things” are cleansed with blood by the law (Heb 9:22). Even this flour is burnt on top of the offerings of blood on the altar (Lev 5:12), and the writer's conclusion stands: “without shedding of blood there is no forgiveness” (Heb 9:22), and the law's offerings were a shadow that could not take away sins (Heb 10:1–4).

note: Drafted 2026-11-13 for Leviticus 23 and Numbers 10 (סֹלֶת, Lev 23:13, 17). Root key: the database files סֹלֶת (o.bs.ab) under root סלק by BDB's page order (entry_root and word_info both give סלק; the lexicon_entry cons is סלת). BDB's own heading is a separate root סלת, and סלק “go up” (o.bs.aa, Psa 139:8; Aramaic סְלֵק xo.ae.aa) has nothing to do with flour, so the entry takes the word's own consonants, סלת, as a noun with no verbal root. The app still finds it for סֹלֶת tokens through the BDB-key fallback; if a סלק entry is ever written, its root lookup would take the סֹלֶת tokens, so the corpus root of o.bs.ab should be corrected to סלת. Words: only סֹלֶת; the verb סִלֵּת “sift” is post-biblical (Mishnah) and not entered. Left out under root סלק in the database, as other roots: סָלֵק/סְלֵק “go up”, סְמָדַר “blossom” and the name Samgar-nebo (o.bs.ad, a Babylonian officer, Jer 39:3), none of them this word. Token count: the brief lists 53 references (Num 28:12 twice). Not entered: Egyptian ṯr.t (Wiktionary compares it, as a likely loan from Semitic into Egyptian; the schema has no place for a loan out of Hebrew into Egyptian, and TLA was not checked). Leads not followed: Syriac (Payne Smith, Brockelmann) for a סלת form; the Peshitta Old Testament's word for סֹלֶת (likely ܣܡܝܕܐ, from the different word behind σεμίδαλις, not this root); CAD S for siltu. Open: whether ar-salata “strip off” is the root's older sense (recorded possible).
